t: and/ I will take my stand

x.ASV: I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower, and will look forth to see what he will speak with me, and what I shall answer concerning my complaint.
x.Darby: I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower, and will look forth to see what he will say unto me, and what I shall answer as to my reproof.
x.KJV: I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower, and will watch to see what he will say unto me, and what I shall answer when I am reproved.
x.YLT: On my charge I stand, and I station myself on a bulwark, and I watch to see what He doth speak against me, and what I do reply to my reproof.

nt: Habakkuk is speaking of his act of waiting for God’s reply as if he were a guard standing at a **watchtower**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will wait attentively for what God will say to me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **complaint**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what I am complaining about]

x.ASV: And Jehovah answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain upon tablets, that he may run that readeth it.
x.Darby: And Jehovah answered me and said, Write the vision, and engrave it upon tablets, that he may run that readeth it.
x.KJV: And the Lord answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it.
x.YLT: And Jehovah answereth me and saith: `Write a vision, and explain on the tables, That he may run who is reading it.

nt: The phrase **and said** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly. Alternate translation: [Then Yahweh answered me,]
וַ⁠יַּעֲנֵ֤⁠נִי יְהוָה֙ וַ⁠יֹּ֔אמֶר כְּת֣וֹב חָז֔וֹן וּ⁠בָאֵ֖ר עַל־הַ⁠לֻּח֑וֹת

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Then Yahweh answered me and told me to write the vision and to make it plain on the tablets] or [Then Yahweh answered me, telling me to write the vision and make it plain on the tablets]

Here, **so that** marks **the one reading it may run** as the goal or purpose of writing the vision and making it plain on the tablets. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [in order that the one reading it may run]

Here, **run** represents the urgent heralding response of the one who reads the message. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the one reading it may hasten to proclaim it]

x.ASV: For the vision is yet for the appointed time, and it hasteth toward the end, and shall not lie: though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not delay.
x.Darby: For the vision is yet for an appointed time, but it hasteth to the end, and shall not lie: though it tarry, wait for it; for it will surely come, it will not delay.
x.KJV: For the vision is yet for an appointed time, but at the end it shall speak, and not lie: though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not tarry.
x.YLT: For yet the vision is for a season, And it breatheth for the end, and doth not lie, If it tarry, wait for it, For surely it cometh, it is not late.

nt: וְ⁠יָפֵ֥חַ לַ⁠קֵּ֖ץ וְ⁠לֹ֣א יְכַזֵּ֑ב אִם־יִתְמַהְמָהּ֙ חַכֵּה־ל֔⁠וֹ כִּֽי־בֹ֥א יָבֹ֖א לֹ֥א יְאַחֵֽר

Yahweh is speaking of **the vision** as if it were a living thing that could **speak** about the end, **lie**, tarry, and **delay**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [it is a message about the end that will certainly prove true; even if its fulfillment seems slow in coming, it will surely be fulfilled at the appointed time]

The author uses the word **Though** here to indicate a contrast between the possibility that the vision may seem delayed and the certainty that it will come eventually. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Even if it tarries, wait for it] or [Even if it seems to be delayed, do not give up waiting for it]

This is an imperative, but it communicates an exhortation or encouragement rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates encouragement. Alternate translation: [you should wait for it]

The author is repeating forms of the verb **come** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [it will certainly come]

x.ASV: Behold, his soul is puffed up, it is not upright in him; but the righteous shall live by his faith.
x.Darby: Behold, his soul is puffed up, it is not upright within him: but the just shall live by his faith.
x.KJV: Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him: but the just shall live by his faith.
x.YLT: Lo, a presumptuous one! Not upright is his soul within him, And the righteous by his stedfastness liveth.

nt: The author is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look!]

Here the author is speaking of a proud person as if his **soul** were something that could be physically **puffed up** or inflated. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He is arrogant]

Here, **soul** represents the entire person from the perspective of his inner character. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [He himself]

The pronouns **His** and **him** both refer to the proud, arrogant person described in this verse, who is contrasted with **the righteous** in the following clause. In the context of the book, this probably means the Chaldeans. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state this explicitly. Alternate translation: [The Chaldeans’ souls are puffed up; it is not upright within them]

The expression **is puffed up** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [has become proud]

Here the author is speaking of moral character as if it were something that could be physically **upright** or straight. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his character is not right within him]

The author is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the righteous person]

The author uses the word **but** here to indicate a contrast between the proud person whose soul is not upright and the righteous person who lives by faithfulness. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [however, the righteous person will live by his faithfulness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [being faithful to God]

x.ASV: Yea, moreover, wine is treacherous, a haughty man, that keepeth not at home; who enlargeth his desire as Sheol, and he is as death, and cannot be satisfied, but gathereth unto him all nations, and heapeth unto him all peoples.
x.Darby: And moreover, the wine is treacherous: he is a proud man, and keepeth not at rest, he enlargeth his desire as Sheol, and he is like death and cannot be satisfied; and he assembleth unto him all nations, and gathereth unto him all peoples.
x.KJV: Yea also, because he transgresseth by wine, he is a proud man, neither keepeth at home, who enlargeth his desire as hell, and is as death, and cannot be satisfied, but gathereth unto him all nations, and heapeth unto him all people:
x.YLT: And also, because the wine is treacherous, A man is haughty, and remaineth not at home, Who hath enlarged as sheol his soul, And is as death that is not satisfied, And doth gather unto itself all the nations, And doth assemble unto itself all the peoples,

nt: The point of this comparison is that just as **Sheol** is never full and always takes in more of the dead, so the arrogant warrior is never content and always desires more conquests. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [who makes his desire as vast as the grave]

Yahweh is speaking of **wine** as if it were a person capable of betraying or deceiving someone. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [wine causes the arrogant warrior to go astray]
אֲשֶׁר֩ הִרְחִ֨יב כִּ⁠שְׁא֜וֹל נַפְשׁ֗⁠וֹ וְ⁠ה֤וּא כַ⁠מָּ֨וֶת֙ וְ⁠לֹ֣א יִשְׂבָּ֔ע

See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of clauses in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [whose appetite is never filled, like Sheol and death]

Here, **appetite** represents desire or craving. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [his desire] or [his sense of need]

The point of this comparison is that just as **death** is relentless and never stops taking people, so this person is relentless and **never satisfied** in his greed. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [he is as relentless as death and is never satisfied]
וַ⁠יֶּאֱסֹ֤ף אֵלָי⁠ו֙ כָּל־הַ⁠גּוֹיִ֔ם וַ⁠יִּקְבֹּ֥ץ אֵלָ֖י⁠ו כָּל־הָ⁠עַמִּֽים

See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of clauses in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [And he gathers to himself every nation and every people] or [And he gathers to himself all of the nations; yes, he collects for himself all of the peoples]

x.ASV: Shall not all these take up a parable against him, and a taunting proverb against him, and say, Woe to him that increaseth that which is not his! how long? and that ladeth himself with pledges!
x.Darby: Shall not all these take up a proverb about him, and a taunting riddle against him, and say, Woe to him that increaseth that which is not his! how long? — and to him that loadeth himself with pledges!
x.KJV: Shall not all these take up a parable against him, and a taunting proverb against him, and say, Woe to him that increaseth that which is not his! how long? and to him that ladeth himself with thick clay!
x.YLT: Do not these--all of them--against him a simile taken up, And a moral of acute sayings for him, And say, Woe to him who is multiplying what is not his? Till when also is he multiplying to himself heavy pledges?

nt: הֲ⁠לוֹא־אֵ֣לֶּה כֻלָּ֗⁠ם עָלָי⁠ו֙ מָשָׁ֣ל יִשָּׂ֔אוּ וּ⁠מְלִיצָ֖ה חִיד֣וֹת ל֑⁠וֹ וְ⁠יֹאמַ֗ר ה֚וֹי הַ⁠מַּרְבֶּ֣ה לֹּא־ל֔⁠וֹ עַד־מָתַ֕י וּ⁠מַכְבִּ֥יד עָלָ֖י⁠ו עַבְטִֽיט

Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that the conquered peoples will certainly mock the oppressor. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [These, all of them, will certainly take up a proverb against him, and ridicule, a riddle about him, so that it says, ‘Woe to the one increasing what is not his’—‘until when? and loading onto himself pledges’!]
וְ⁠יֹאמַ֗ר ה֚וֹי הַ⁠מַּרְבֶּ֣ה לֹּא־ל֔⁠וֹ עַד־מָתַ֕י וּ⁠מַכְבִּ֥יד עָלָ֖י⁠ו עַבְטִֽיט

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [so that it pronounces woe on the one increasing what is not his—until when? and loading onto himself pledges]
ה֚וֹי הַ⁠מַּרְבֶּ֣ה לֹּא־ל֔⁠וֹ עַד־מָתַ֕י וּ⁠מַכְבִּ֥יד עָלָ֖י⁠ו עַבְטִֽיט

Here the conquered peoples use a proverb in order to mock the greedy conqueror. Translate this proverb in a way that will be recognized as a proverb and be meaningful in your language and culture. Alternate translation: [Disaster awaits the one who endlessly takes what does not belong to him and burdens himself with debts]

The conquered peoples are interjecting this brief question form to express frustration that the oppressor’s greed has continued for too long. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [for far too long!]

x.ASV: Shall they not rise up suddenly that shall bite thee, and awake that shall vex thee, and thou shalt be for booty unto them?
x.Darby: Shall they not rise up suddenly that shall bite thee, and they awake up that shall vex thee, and thou shalt be for booties unto them?
x.KJV: Shall they not rise up suddenly that shall bite thee, and awake that shall vex thee, and thou shalt be for booties unto them?
x.YLT: Do not thy usurers instantly rise up, And those shaking thee awake up, And thou hast been for a spoil to them?

nt: Here the author is introducing **your biters** as new participants. The phrase refers to the people whom the oppressor has exploited, who will now turn against him. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Will not those whom you oppressed suddenly rise up]
הֲ⁠ל֣וֹא פֶ֗תַע יָק֨וּמוּ֙ נֹשְׁכֶ֔י⁠ךָ וְ⁠יִקְצ֖וּ מְזַעְזְעֶ֑י⁠ךָ

The author is using the question form to emphasize that those who oppose the oppressor will certainly rebel. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Your biters will suddenly rise up, and the ones shaking you will awaken!]

The Hebrew word translated **biters** could mean: (1) your creditors, that is, the plundered peoples who will demand repayment as if they were animals that bite. Alternate translation: [your creditors] (2) those who you have oppressed by forcing them to pay you unjustly. Alternate translation: [those you forced to be in debt to you]

Here the author is speaking of those who will demand payment as if they were people who were **shaking** someone. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones who will make you tremble]

Here the author is speaking of the oppressor as if he were plunder that could be taken as **spoils** of war. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Then they will take everything from you]

x.ASV: Because thou hast plundered many nations, all the remnant of the peoples shall plunder thee, because of men’s blood, and for the violence done to the land, to the city and to all that dwell therein.
x.Darby: Because thou hast plundered many nations, all the rest of the peoples shall plunder thee; because of men's blood, and for the violence [done] to the land, to the city, and all that dwell therein.
x.KJV: Because thou hast spoiled many nations, all the remnant of the people shall spoil thee; because of men’s blood, and for the violence of the land, of the city, and of all that dwell therein.
x.YLT: Because thou hast spoiled many nations, Spoil thee do all the remnant of the peoples, Because of man's blood, and of violence to the land, To the city, and to all dwelling in it.

nt: מִ⁠דְּמֵ֤י אָדָם֙ וַ⁠חֲמַס־אֶ֔רֶץ קִרְיָ֖ה וְ⁠כָל־יֹ֥שְׁבֵי בָֽ⁠הּ

Here the author is clarifying who suffered from the oppressor’s actions. The phrase identifies the victims and the places that were harmed. Your language may have its own way of specifying the victims that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [because of the people you murdered and the violent way you treated the land, the city, and all who live in it]

Here, **bloodshed** represents the act of murdering people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [because of your murderous ways]

x.ASV: Woe to him that getteth an evil gain for his house, that he may set his nest on high, that he may be delivered from the hand of evil!
x.Darby: Woe to him that getteth iniquitous gain to his house, that he may set his nest on high, that he may be delivered from the grasp of evil!
x.KJV: Woe to him that coveteth an evil covetousness to his house, that he may set his nest on high, that he may be delivered from the power of evil!
x.YLT: Woe to him who is gaining evil gain for his house, To set on high his nest, To be delivered from the hand of evil,

nt: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [They will say that terrible things will happen to the one gaining an evil gain for his house]

The phrase **Woe to the one gaining an evil gain for his house** expresses a strong feeling of warning and coming judgment. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [How terrible it will be for the one gaining an evil gain for his house]

The author is repeating forms of the word **gain** in order to intensify the idea of greedy, exploitative profit. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [the one greedily getting evil profit]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **an evil gain**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [money evilly]

Here the author is speaking of the oppressor building his house in a secure, elevated place as if he were a bird setting **his nest on high**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to make his dwelling secure in a high place]

The expression **to be delivered** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [to deliver himself]

Here, **hand** represents the power or control of evil. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the power of evil]

The author is using the possessive form to describe a **hand** that is characterized by **evil**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from the evil grasp]

x.ASV: Thou hast devised shame to thy house, by cutting off many peoples, and hast sinned against thy soul.
x.Darby: Thou hast devised shame to thy house, by cutting off many peoples, and hast sinned against thine own soul.
x.KJV: Thou hast consulted shame to thy house by cutting off many people, and hast sinned against thy soul.
x.YLT: Thou hast counselled a shameful thing to thy house, To cut off many peoples, and sinful is thy soul.

nt: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **shame**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what is shameful]

Habakkuk is speaking of destroying nations as if it were **cutting** them **off**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [destroying many peoples]
Here, **soul** represents the person himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [sinning against yourself]

x.ASV: For the stone shall cry out of the wall, and the beam out of the timber shall answer it.
x.Darby: For the stone shall cry out of the wall, and the beam out of the timber shall answer it.
x.KJV: For the stone shall cry out of the wall, and the beam out of the timber shall answer it.
x.YLT: For a stone from the wall doth cry out, And a holdfast from the wood answereth it.

nt: אֶ֖בֶן מִ⁠קִּ֣יר תִּזְעָ֑ק וְ⁠כָפִ֖יס מֵ⁠עֵ֥ץ יַעֲנֶֽ⁠נָּה

The author is speaking of **a stone** and **a beam** as if they were living things that could **cry out** and **answer**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [even the stolen stones in your wall and the wooden beams are evidence of your wrongdoing]

x.ASV: Woe to him that buildeth a town with blood, and establisheth a city by iniquity!
x.Darby: Woe to him that buildeth a town with blood, and establisheth a city by unrighteousness!
x.KJV: Woe to him that buildeth a town with blood, and stablisheth a city by iniquity!
x.YLT: Woe to him who is building a city by blood, And establishing a city by iniquity.

nt: The word **Woe** here communicates a warning about coming disaster. If a speaker of your language would not express this as an exclamation, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Terrible things will happen to the one building a city with bloodshed]

The author is not referring to one specific person but to anyone who does this. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this idea using a different form. Alternate translation: [anyone who builds a city]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **bloodshed**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by working people so hard they die]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **injustice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by acting unjustly]

x.ASV: Behold, is it not of Jehovah of hosts that the peoples labor for the fire, and the nations weary themselves for vanity?
x.Darby: Behold, is it not of Jehovah of hosts that the peoples labour for the fire, and the nations weary themselves in vain?
x.KJV: Behold, is it not of the Lord of hosts that the people shall labour in the very fire, and the people shall weary themselves for very vanity?
x.YLT: Lo, is it not from Jehovah of Hosts And peoples are fatigued for fire, And nations for vanity are weary?

nt: The author is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use here. Alternate translation: [Pay attention]
הֲ⁠ל֣וֹא הִנֵּ֔ה מֵ⁠אֵ֖ת יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֑וֹת וְ⁠יִֽיגְע֤וּ עַמִּים֙ בְּ⁠דֵי־אֵ֔שׁ וּ⁠לְאֻמִּ֖ים בְּ⁠דֵי־רִ֥יק יִעָֽפוּ

The author is using the question form to emphasize that this is certainly true. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement. Alternate translation: [Behold, it is from Yahweh of armies that peoples labor for fire and nations weary themselves for emptiness.]

Here the author is speaking as if the results of people’s work were fuel that would be consumed by **fire**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use here, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that peoples work hard for nothing]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **emptiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for nothing]

x.ASV: For the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of Jehovah, as the waters cover the sea.
x.Darby: For the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of Jehovah as the waters cover the sea.
x.KJV: For the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea.
x.YLT: For full is the earth of the knowledge of the honour of Jehovah, As waters cover the bottom of a sea.

nt: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [God will fill the earth]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with people who know how glorious Yahweh is]

The author is using the possessive form to describe **glory** that belongs to **Yahweh**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s glory]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the waters** completely **cover over the sea**, so the knowledge of Yahweh’s glory will completely fill the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [just as water completely fills the ocean]

x.ASV: Woe unto him that giveth his neighbor drink, to thee that addest thy venom, and makest him drunken also, that thou mayest look on their nakedness!
x.Darby: Woe unto him that giveth his neighbour drink, — that pourest out thy flask, and makest [him] drunken also, that thou mayest look on their nakedness!
x.KJV: Woe unto him that giveth his neighbour drink, that puttest thy bottle to him, and makest him drunken also, that thou mayest look on their nakedness!
x.YLT: Woe to him who is giving drink to his neighbour, Pouring out thy bottle, and also making drunk, In order to look on their nakedness.

nt: The word **Woe** here communicates a warning about coming disaster. If a speaker of your language would not express this as an exclamation, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Terrible things will happen to the one causing his neighbor to drink]

Habakkuk is not referring to one specific person but to anyone who does this. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this idea using a different form. Alternate translation: [anyone who causes his neighbor to drink]
מַשְׁקֵ֣ה רֵעֵ֔⁠הוּ מְסַפֵּ֥חַ חֲמָתְ⁠ךָ֖ וְ⁠אַ֣ף שַׁכֵּ֑ר

Here the author is speaking of exploiting and humiliating other nations as if it were **causing** them **to drink** and **making** them **drunk**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use here, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one exploiting the vulnerability of his neighbor, intoxicating him, and promoting his drunkenness]

Habakkuk has been speaking about the oppressor in the third person (**his** neighbor) but shifts to addressing him directly in the second person with **your**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use consistent pronouns throughout. Alternate translation: [pouring out his wineskin]

Here, **in order to** marks **look upon their nakedness** as the goal or purpose of **causing his neighbor to drink** and **making him drunk**.
